paras: The Pocahontas moonshiner raid was an armed incursion into Pocahontas, Virginia, on a Sunday in late July 1890, apparently July 20, by a band of about twenty men from West Virginia who got drunk and fired on passers-by. Two Black residents, one of them Charles Smith, were seriously wounded before town officers fought off the band, captured two of its members and drove the rest back across the state line. Newspapers as far away as Kansas, South Carolina and Georgia carried the story as a moonshiners' raid and a "border war."

Pocahontas lay near the West Virginia line, and the raiders were described as a gang of "desperadoes" with their headquarters in the West Virginia mountains. A Charleston dispatch named their leader as "the notorious Jim Skinner, the well-known moonshiner," while a Lynchburg dispatch said only that they were "a party of men from McDowell County, W. Va."

Early in the afternoon the band rode into the town and began drinking whiskey. Within a few hours they were flourishing their revolvers and, in the Charleston dispatch's words, "firing at negroes as they passed"; another printing of the same dispatch said "on citizens." Two colored men were seriously wounded, among them Charles Smith, a resident of Pocahontas who was shot in the head and arms.

The town sergeant then summoned a posse and tried to arrest the raiders, who opened fire and, according to the Lynchburg report, wounded several of his men. In the general fight that followed, two of the band were shot and captured and lodged in jail, and the rest fled over the state line into West Virginia.

That evening, or on Monday night by the Charleston account, a rumor spread that the band would return to rescue the prisoners. The mayor ordered out a posse of sixty men to patrol the town, which the Lynchburg dispatch described as calling out "the military." The coverage does not report whether the captured men were tried or whether the wounded men recovered.

Only white papers carried the story, in two separate dispatches dated July 23 at Lynchburg and July 24 at Charleston, West Virginia. The Iola Register in Kansas ran the Lynchburg version on August 1 under the headline "Border War," telling it as a battle between "invaders" and the town's officers without mentioning the Black victims. The Charleston version ran the same day in the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer as "Moonshiners Raid a Town," was reprinted word for word in the Abbeville Press and Banner on August 6, and appeared with its dateline in the Thomas County Cat of Georgia on August 7 as "A Bloody Fight."

In every version the raiders, called "desperadoes" and "the mob," were the story, and the wounded Black men appeared in a single sentence, with Smith described as "an unknown negro" in the Georgia printing. No paper stated the raiders' race or gave a motive beyond drink, and no Black-press coverage of the raid was found.

The two dispatches differ on who was hurt: the Charleston report names two colored passers-by and two wounded raiders, while the Lynchburg report mentions only wounded members of the sergeant's posse. The Georgia printing's phrase "Charles Smith an unknown negro resident" can be read as naming one man, though the same text says two colored men were wounded.

reader.title: Pocahontas moonshiner raid
bases: An armed band of about twenty men rode into the town, drank, and fired on passers-by, seriously wounding two colored men, before town authorities drove it off (A1, A4); no one was reported killed and no lynching or seizure of a prisoner was reported (A2).

Two separate dispatches, one from Charleston, W. Va. (A1, A4) and one from Lynchburg, Va. (A2), agree that an armed party rode into Pocahontas, fired in the streets, fought the town authorities, lost two men captured and fled into West Virginia, and that a rescue rumor led the mayor to call out armed men.

accounts.label: Charleston, W. Va., dispatch
accounts.gist: About twenty desperadoes under moonshiner Jim Skinner rode into Pocahontas, got drunk and fired at Black passers-by, seriously wounding two colored men including Charles Smith; citizens and authorities fought them, captured two, and the rest fled to West Virginia.

accounts.label: Lynchburg, Va., dispatch
accounts.gist: Men from McDowell County, W. Va., fired 'promiscuously' in the streets and wounded several of the town sergeant's posse when it tried to arrest them; two were jailed and the rest escaped over the state line. It does not mention Black victims.

framing.detail: 'Moonshiners Raid a Town' calls the raiders 'desperadoes' and 'the mob' and says they fired 'on citizens', naming the wounded as colored men.
'Border War' frames the affair as an invasion across the state line and an armed battle with the town officers, naming no race.
Reprints the 'Moonshiners Raid a Town' text unchanged beneath an unrelated Labrador murder story.
'A Bloody Fight' prints the Charleston dispatch with its date and says the band fired 'at negroes as they passed'.
